h: לְאַרְבָּעָה עָשָׂר אֲדָר רִאשׁוֹן, מַאֲמָר א׳ For the Fourteenth of Adar Rishon — Maamar Aleph

p: In the Shulchan Aruch, Orach Chaim
on the fourteenth of Adar Rishon,
וְטוֹב לֵב מִשְׁתֶּה תָמִיד [מִשְׁלֵי טו, טו]
"And one of good heart has a constant feast" (Mishlei 15:15).
It was already written in the sefer Urim VeTumim
[קִיצּוּר תּוֹקְפוֹ כֹּהֵן אוֹת קכג קכד בְּסוֹפוֹ]
(Kitzur Tokfo Kohen, os 123–124, at the end)
that we may interpret the wording of the Shulchan Aruch
even if they did not intend this,
for in any case the true matter
which were written with ruach hakodesh.
So too here, where he concluded with this pasuk,
אַף דִּלְכְאוֹרָה אֵין לוֹ שַׁיָּכוּת לְכָאן
even though it seemingly has no connection to this place
but only serves to conclude with something good.
that in its plain sense it is not understood
מַה שֶּׁנֶּאֱמַר וְטוֹב לֵב מִשְׁתֶּה תָמִיד
what is said, "And one of good heart has a constant feast" —
does then one whose heart is good
as referring to one who is happy with his lot,
וּכְאִלּוּ נִכְתָּב וְטוֹב לֵב כְּמִשְׁתֶּה תָמִיד
as if it were written, "one of good heart is like a constant feast,"
and it is not a statement and its opposite
"All the days of the poor man are bad,"
rather it refers to the poor man himself:
when he is happy with his lot
he is like a constant feast.
But this too needs to be understood:
is a constant feast then a virtue?
There are many pesukim in Mishlei
is that he is always joyful,
He saw that he was very merry,
and said to him, "In all sorrow
דְּטוֹב לֵב הוּא מִי שֶׁלִּבּוֹ טוֹב
that "good of heart" is one whose heart is good,
who has emptied out the yetzer hara
from "the heart of the fool, at his left,"
and he has only a good heart,
one heart to his Father in Heaven,
so that the left heart too has become good,
and he is always in joy.
"On that day Hashem will be One" —
is He then not One nowadays?
it is all "Who is good and does good,"
that there are no bad tidings there;
there is the opposite of good,
and then this will not be,
for they will recognize the good.
In truth, even in this world
truly feels at the time of Krias Shema
that it is all "Who is good and does good,"
meaning that everything is for the good,
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמַר רַבִּי עֲקִיבָא (בְּרָכוֹת ס, ב)
A person should always be accustomed to say,
And Rabbi Akiva showed them immediately
that all that is done is for the good,
and said to them, "Did I not tell you
שֶׁכָּל מַה שֶּׁעוֹשֶׂה הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא
that all that the Holy One, blessed is He, does
This is unlike what he said earlier (Berachos ibid.),
meaning that even though he knows it is not good,
לְאָדָם שֶׁיָּצָא עָלָיו שְׁטַר חוֹב וְכוּלֵּי
"Like a man against whom a promissory note came out...
after he paid it, he rejoiced."
But the attribute of Rabbi Akiva was
that he recognized that the event is truly for the good
and is not in the category of bad at all,
just as they will recognize in the World to Come
that it is all "Who is good and does good."
This is "and one of good heart":
who eradicates the evil from the heart of the fool —
for he is always in joy.
"and drink of the wine I have mixed" —
the wine of the Oral Torah,
as they said in the Ra'aya Mehemna
that it is all "Who is good and does good,"
כֵּיוָן שֶׁמְּתַקֵּן עַל יְדֵי הָרוֹב חָכְמָה
since through the abundance of wisdom he rectifies
from "the heart of the fool, at his left."
for it is found in the Midrash
כָּל יְקָר רָאֲתָה עֵינוֹ [אִיּוֹב כח, י]
"His eye has seen every precious thing" (Iyov 28:10) —
this is Rabbi Akiva and his colleagues;
things that were not revealed to Moshe
were revealed to Rabbi Akiva and his colleagues,
for he was the root of Torah she'b'al peh
this perception at the time of Krias Shema,
that it is all "Who is good and does good,"
and then he is joyful in the heart.
Therefore when he said to him,
"It is written, 'In all sorrow there will be profit,'"
he answered him, "I am wearing tefillin" —
for the essence of the mitzvah of tefillin
is to perceive the Unity of "Hashem is One,"
that it is all "Who is good and does good."
at the time of Krias Shema always,
and when he merits perceiving the Unity,
for he recognizes that everything is for the good.
This was the root of the miracle of Purim,
which is the time of the eradication of Amalek,
who is the root of the evil inclination,
as they said in the holy Zohar
for were it not for the decree there would have been no way
to carry out the eradication of Amalek
and to kill from among his people;
they, over those who hated them."
and it was not an evil decree
but only a cause for good,
so that they could carry out the eradication of Amalek.
This is unlike the redemption from Egypt,
where at the time of the trouble it was truly trouble,
and only afterward were they redeemed from it
they recognized that it was for the good from the outset,
the lot was for our benefit,
so that we could carry out the eradication of Amalek,
מַה שֶּׁלֹּא הָיָה אֶפְשָׁר בְּלָאו הָכִי.
which would not have been possible otherwise.
Now the root of the dispute
on the fourteenth of Adar Rishon
is that in the Gemara (Megillah 6b) it states:
אֵין בֵּין אַרְבָּעָה עָשָׂר שֶׁבַּאֲדָר רִאשׁוֹן
There is no difference between the fourteenth of Adar Rishon
and the fourteenth of Adar Sheni
except the reading of the Megillah
Feasting and rejoicing are not mentioned,
(on the Rif there, 3b in the Rif's pages,
that since the prohibition of eulogy and fasting
"rejoicing" — that they are forbidden in eulogy;
"feasting" — that it is forbidden to fast;
the obligation of feasting and rejoicing
on the fourteenth of Adar Rishon is included
within the prohibition of eulogy and fasting
(מְגִילָּה ו, ב דִּבּוּר הַמַּתְחִיל וְרַבִּי) כָּתְבוּ
דְּכֵיוָן דְּאָמְרוּ הָא לְעִנְיַן הֶסְפֵּד וְתַעֲנִית
that since they said, "but regarding eulogy and fasting
this implies that rejoicing and feasting do not apply in the first,
דְּעַל כָּרְחָךְ לָא תַּלְיָא הָא בְּהָא
for perforce the one does not depend on the other,
for otherwise it should have taught us
that feasting and rejoicing are practiced in it,
and all the more so that it is forbidden in eulogy;
And according to the view of Tosafos one must understand:
מְנָא לְהוּ לְמֵיסַר הֶסְפֵּד וְתַעֲנִית בְּרִאשׁוֹן
from where do they derive to forbid eulogy and fasting in the first,
since the prohibition of eulogy and fasting
is learned from what is said, "feasting and rejoicing,"
וְזֶה גּוּפֵיהּ אֵינוֹ נוֹהֵג בַּאֲדָר רִאשׁוֹן
and that itself does not apply in Adar Rishon?
And in the Megillah it is written only
רַק לַעֲשׂוֹת אוֹתָם יְמֵי מִשְׁתֶּה וְשִׂמְחָה
"to make them days of feasting and rejoicing
and these mitzvos do not apply
on the fourteenth of Adar Rishon;
so from where does he derive to forbid eulogy and fasting?
גַּם יִקְשֶׁה לְשׁוֹן אֵין בֵּין וְכוּלֵּי
Also the wording "there is no difference..." is difficult
regarding the prohibition of eulogy and fasting
in which they are the same,
since all the mitzvos explicitly stated in the Megillah
on the fourteenth of Adar Rishon;
וְאֵיךְ שַׁיָּיךְ לוֹמַר אֵין בֵּין וְכוּלֵּי
so how can one say "there is no difference..."
about the prohibition of eulogy and fasting,
which is not stated explicitly in the Megillah at all?
that they apply only in the second
is either because of the reason
that juxtaposing redemption to redemption is preferable,
or because it is written (Esther 9:29), "to establish
as they said in the Gemara (Megillah 6b);
and so wrote the Targum Sheni
If the year is a leap year,
they shall not read the Megillah
עוֹשִׂים אֶת יוֹם וְגוֹמֵר [אֶסְתֵּר שָׁם יט]
"to establish upon them that they make
"to make them days of feasting and rejoicing
לִהְיוֹת עוֹשִׂים אֶת שְׁנֵי הַיָּמִים וְגוֹמֵר [שָׁם, כז].
And regarding this it is written,
לְקַיֵּים אֵת אִגֶּרֶת הַפּוּרִים הַזֹּאת הַשֵּׁנִית
"to establish this second letter of Purim":
that to fulfill in deed the reading of the Megillah,
sending portions and gifts to the poor,
they instituted only in Adar Sheni
and to this the reason applies
that juxtaposing redemption to redemption is preferable,
with regard to the enactment in deed.
Reading the Megillah and gifts to the poor
are in deed, the revelation of the miracle
that was performed for our forefathers at this season,
and this applies only in the second.
But the root of the mitzvos in the heart —
are called by the name "the month of Adar,"
and when this season comes in Adar Rishon
it too is a time of the eradication of Amalek —
a person feels in the heart
the aspect of feasting and rejoicing and good heart,
that they can rectify "the heart of the fool, at his left,"
for this is the essence of the eradication of Amalek,
as we cited from the holy Zohar.
Consequently it is forbidden in eulogy and fasting,
כֵּיוָן שֶׁהוּא זְמַן מִשְׁתֶּה וְשִׂמְחָה בַּלֵּב
since it is a time of feasting and rejoicing in the heart;
זְמַן הִתְגַּלּוּת אוֹר תּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה
a time of the revelation of the light of Torah she'b'al peh.
and they expounded (Megillah 16b): this is Torah,
which is called orah, in the feminine,
since it receives from the Written Torah,
And through the abundance of wisdom
one merits to rectify the abundance of anger,
that is, to uproot and extirpate the evil
from "the heart of the fool, at his left,"
וְלִהְיוֹת לוֹ רַק לֵב אֶחָד לֵב טוֹב
and to have only one heart, a good heart;
"and one of good heart has a constant feast,"
and he feels the joy in the heart
שֶׁכָּל מַה שֶּׁהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא עוֹשֶׂה
that all that the Holy One, blessed is He, does
just as they will recognize in the World to Come
that it is all "Who is good and does good."
שֶׁעַל זֶה נִזְכַּר בַּמְּגִילָּה [אֶסְתֵּר ט, טז]
For regarding this the Megillah mentions (Esther 9:16)
"as the days on which the Jews rested
meaning the rest in the heart,
in the manner they said in the holy Zohar
"On the day Hashem gives you rest...
that even when he is in hard labor
he has rest in the heart,
that everything is for the good.
that the decree was for the good,
So too "sending portions one to another"
is so that all should be
as one man with one heart.
תִּקְּנוּ רַק בְּאַרְבָּעָה עָשָׂר שֶׁבַּאֲדָר הַשֵּׁנִי
they instituted only on the fourteenth of Adar Sheni,
but in the heart one must,
so that all of Yisrael be
as one man with one heart,
the revelation of the light of Torah.
As at the Giving of the Torah,
as found in the Mechilta (Yisro, Parashas BaChodesh 1):
וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה זָכוּ לְמַתַּן תּוֹרָה
and through this they merited the Giving of the Torah.
they become as one man with one heart,
And this applies in the heart
even on the fourteenth of Adar Rishon,
which is also a time of the revelation
of Torah she'b'al peh, as mentioned above.
only the reading of the Megillah and gifts to the poor,
and the Mishnah does not mention sending portions
as applying only in the second.
וְהָרַ״ן לֹא כָּתַב טַעַם עַל זֶה
The Ran did not write a reason for this,
and wrote that since they resemble gifts to the poor,
which apply only in the second,
וּלְפִי זֶה לָמָּה לֹא חָשְׁבוּ בַּמִּשְׁנָה.
But according to this, why did they not list it in the Mishnah?
According to what we have said,
which are only charity in deed,
is to be as one man with one heart —
even on the fourteenth of Adar Rishon:
that all of Yisrael be companions
וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה לַיְּהוּדִים הָיְתָה אוֹרָה
And through this "the Jews had light":
alluding to "drink of the wine I have mixed."
And "gladness" — that he feel and perceive the light,
"Hashem is One," and all is for the good.
This is "and one of good heart":
וְאֵין לוֹ רַק לֵב אֶחָד טוֹב
and he has only one good heart —
for he feels the Unity, "Hashem is One,"
that it is all "Who is good and does good."
And on Shabbos, which is a semblance of the World to Come
even when he is in hard labor,
as we said from the holy Zohar.
And talmidei chachamim, who resemble Shabbosos,
as they said in the holy Zohar
the revelation of the light of Torah she'b'al peh,
that it is all "Who is good and does good,"
at the time of Krias Shema and when he puts on tefillin,
can perceive the Unity for the moment,
that it is all "Who is good and does good."
וּבְיוֹם זֶה שֶׁהוּא זְמַן מְחִיַּית עֲמָלֵק
And on this day, which is the time of the eradication of Amalek,
when they can eradicate the evil from the heart of the fool
and have only a good heart,
and the joy in the heart.
and the fourteenth of Adar Sheni,
and this is why the Rema concluded on this:
"And one of good heart has a constant feast."

paragraphs.text: Shulchan Aruch and Rema, Orach Chaim 697:1 — “On the fourteenth and fifteenth of AdarI one does not fall on one's face in supplication and does not recite May Hashem answer you in the day of distress. They are forbidden for eulogy and fasting, but the other observances do not apply. Some permit even eulogy and fasting. Rema: The custom follows the first opinion. Some say one must increase feasting and joy on the fourteenth of AdarI; this is not the custom. Nevertheless, one should add a little to the meal to satisfy those who are stringent. One of good heart has a continual feast.”

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Machshavos Charutz 15 — “The Tumim already noted… that since it was accepted throughout all Yisrael … for all their words are to us complete Torah, within the Torah she'b'al peh.” Rav Tzadok applies the same principle to the siman numbering of the Tur and Shulchan Aruch. He gives its basis: a code accepted by all Yisrael becomes part of the Oral Torah, where nothing happens by chance.

paragraphs.text: Rashi, Mishlei 15:15 — “One of good heart: one whose heart is content with his wealth. A continual feast: all his years seem to him like days of feasting, teaching you that a person should rejoice in his own portion. Our Sages expounded what they expounded in Chelek.”

paragraphs.text: Gittin 68a — “When he came, he inspected the seal, opened the vessel, and found wine. He said: It is written, Wine is a scoffer, strong drink is tumultuous, and whoever strays through it will not become wise; and it is written, Harlotry, wine, and fresh wine take away the heart. He did not drink. When he became thirsty and could no longer bear it, he drank, became intoxicated, and slept.” Ashmedai cites these verses when he initially refuses the wine prepared by Benayahu. Rav Tzadok draws on the verses' negative portrayal of wine before explaining the spiritual meaning of a continual feast.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Pri Tzaddik, Rosh Chodesh Shevat 5 — “The yetzer hara… sits between the heart's two openings … Joy comes only when the yetzer hara is entirely nullified and the heart becomes one heart to its Father in Heaven.” This explains why the Geonim's “removal of the heart” and Chachmoni's “joy of the heart” are one reading. Constant joy belongs only to a heart whose left chamber has also been cleared.

paragraphs.text: Pesachim 50a — “Rabbi Acha bar Chanina said: The World to Come is unlike this world. In this world, over good tidings one says, Blessed is the Good and Beneficent, and over bad tidings one says, Blessed is the true Judge. In the World to Come it is all The Good and Beneficent.” Rav Tzadok understands the future unity as the recognition of the good within what now appears adverse.

paragraphs.text: Berakhot 60b — “Rav Huna said in Rav's name, in Rabbi Meir's name, and it was also taught in Rabbi Akiva's name: A person should always be accustomed to say, Whatever the Merciful One does, He does for the good. Rabbi Akiva was traveling and reached a town, but they gave him no lodging. He said: Whatever the Merciful One does is for the good. He slept in the field, with a rooster, a donkey, and a lamp. Wind extinguished the lamp, a cat ate the rooster, and a lion ate the donkey. He said: Whatever the Merciful One does is for the good. That night an armed troop came and captured the town.” The losses protected Rabbi Akiva from discovery. Rav Tzadok distinguishes recognition of an event's actual good from the separate obligation to accept suffering joyfully.

paragraphs.text: Berakhot 60b — “What does it mean that a person must bless over adversity as he blesses over good? If it means saying The Good and Beneficent over adversity too, did we not learn that over bad tidings one says Blessed is the true Judge? Rava said: The teaching is needed only to require accepting them with joy.”

paragraphs.text: Berakhot 7b — “Rabbi Shimon ben Avishalom said: To what may this be compared? To a person against whom a debt document was issued. Before he paid it, he was sad; after he paid it, he rejoiced.” The Gemara applies this to David's response to punishment involving Avshalom: once his feared punishment had taken a form, he could sing. Rav Tzadok distinguishes this relief from perceiving that the event itself was good.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Rav Tzadok HaKohen, Resisei Layla 9 — “The blessed God is always called the One who bestows good kindnesses, for all His actions and the emanation of all His attributes were only to benefit Israel. ... When it sometimes appears otherwise to the eye, this is, on the contrary, to bestow an even greater goodness beyond human reason. Thus Bereishis Rabbah calls the evil inclination, death, and sleep very good: all appear not good to the eye, yet Scripture says very good, because in them there is a depth of goodness.”

paragraphs.text: Connection: This passage supplies the distinction behind the present discourse: the event may look adverse to ordinary sight while its deeper purpose exceeds that sight. It develops Rav Tzadok's claim that Rabbi Akiva recognized actual good, beyond merely accepting a painful decree.

paragraphs.text: Asher Heini, preserved in Machzor Vitry §248 — “All the world's inhabitants opened their mouths, for Haman's lot was transformed into our lot. The righteous one was rescued from the wicked one's hand; the enemy was given in place of his life. They undertook to observe Purim and rejoice each year.” The liturgical wording is independently preserved in Machzor Vitry's text of Asher Heini. Rav Tzadok uses the transformation of the lot itself to explain how the original decree becomes the means for the rescue.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: R. Moshe Chaim Luzzatto, Da'at Tevunot, section 48, paragraphs 3–4 — “Certainly the Holy One, blessed be He, does not intend to hold to the course of good and evil for a period of time and then abandon it, taking up the course of sovereignty and unity in a single moment like someone who regrets and changes his mind. Rather, in the depth of His counsel He directs events with such profound wisdom that, through good and evil themselves, we finally reach the point where everything is perfected and He reveals His unity. … The conduct of reward and punishment is open and always visible to everyone. But the course through which He turns everything toward the good is exceedingly deep, and becomes manifest only at the end. Yet it is certainly unfolding at every moment and every hour, without ceasing.”

paragraphs.text: Connection: Ramchal describes two modes operating simultaneously: visible judgment and the hidden direction of those very events toward the revelation of unity. This clarifies why Rav Tzadok treats the decree of Haman as the means of the deliverance itself. Its reversal reveals what the decree accomplished within the one divine purpose; it is more than a later benefit added after an unrelated calamity. Purim, in Rav Tzadok's account, allows that hidden connection to be recognized within history.

paragraphs.text: Megillah 5b — “Rav Yosef taught: Joy, feasting, and a festival day. Joy teaches that they are forbidden for eulogy; feasting teaches that fasting is forbidden; a festival day teaches that work is forbidden.” The ensuing discussion explains that the prohibition of work was not accepted. Rav Tzadok's question uses the derivation of eulogy and fasting from joy and feasting.

paragraphs.text: Ran on the Rif, Megillah 3b, s.v. Ela mikra Megillah — “It appears to me that the Mishnah did not also say The Purim feast because the Gemara concludes that the two Adars are alike regarding eulogy and fasting: both are forbidden. The prohibition of eulogy and fasting is derived from joy and feasting, as the Gemara says: Joy teaches that eulogy is forbidden; feasting teaches that fasting is forbidden. This is the basic obligation of the additional meal. ... It is also close to certain that one should increase the meal on the fourteenth of the first Adar. But as to sending portions, since these resemble gifts to the poor, which apply only in the second Adar, it appears that sending portions likewise applies only in the second.”

paragraphs.text: Tosafos, Megillah 6b, s.v. VeRabbi Eliezer — “Some customarily make the fourteenth and fifteenth of the first Adar days of feasting and joy, and the Mishnah's wording seems to imply this. ... This does not appear correct, for the Gemara says that the two are alike regarding eulogy and fasting, implying that joy and feasting do not apply. The one cannot depend upon the other; otherwise it should have taught that feasting and joy apply, from which the prohibition of eulogy would follow automatically. ... The law is that one need not be stringent by making a feast and rejoicing in the first Adar.” Tosafos disagrees with the inference from the prohibition of eulogy and fasting to a positive feast obligation. Rav Tzadok preserves this disagreement and explains a shared inward root.

paragraphs.text: Zohar I 48a–b, Bereishis — “Rabbi Shimon further said: We learned that Shabbos is an image of the World to Come; certainly it is so. Therefore the sabbatical year and the Jubilee correspond to one another, and so do Shabbos and the World to Come. The addition to the soul comes from the mystery of Zachor to this Shelter of Peace, which receives from the World to Come and gives this addition to the holy world. Through that addition they rejoice, and all weekday concerns, pains and troubles are forgotten, as it says, 'On the day Hashem grants you rest from your pain, your turmoil and the hard labor.'” The original in the cited first volume is now matched, including its Isaiah 14:3 proof. It describes Shabbos's addition of soul and release from inner distress. Rav Tzadok applies this rest of the heart to recognizing the good concealed within the Purim decree.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Machshavos Charutz 19 — “The essence of feasting is the bonding of people in love … and the first feast mentioned in the Torah is Lot's for the angels, and through it he was saved.” Rav Tzadok explains there why the whole Purim story turns on feasts. The feast and the sending of portions are means of uniting hearts, so their inner purpose can apply in Adar Rishon as well.

paragraphs.text: Mekhilta, Yisro, BaChodesh 1:23 — “'Israel encamped there'—wherever it says 'they journeyed' and 'they encamped,' they journeyed in dispute and encamped in dispute. But here it says, 'Israel encamped there': they all made their hearts equal as one.” The checked Mekhilta original says 'they all made one heart.' Rav Tzadok expresses the same unity through the familiar 'one man, one heart' wording. Its contrast with earlier disputed encampments supplies the particular unity through which Israel became ready to receive the Torah.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Mei HaShiloach I, Megillah 7a — “When the Men of the Great Assembly investigated where this decree sprang from and found it was from narrowness of eye … afterward they instituted these two mitzvos, whose root is a good eye.” The Izhbitzer gives a parallel account of what mishloach manos repairs. It works on the heart, the root of the decree, which supports Rav Tzadok's point that its intent belongs to the heart rather than to the deed alone.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Pri Tzaddik, Pinchas 17 — “On Shabbos there is rest for Yisrael; even one still in hard labor has rest from everything … then it is all ‘Who is good and does good’; therefore we say ‘You are One.’” Rav Tzadok finds this awareness in the Shabbos Minchah prayer. On Shabbos the oneness of “Hashem is One” is already felt as the goodness of everything, as in the World to Come.
